finding: The per-kind runner map is a required capability of §3.2 ("a map from unit kind to either of those with a `default` key covering the rest", shape discrimination by the presence of `cmd`, "A map missing `default`, or a runner object missing `cmd`, is a usage error") and §3.2.2 adds two more rules for it ("the cap accrues only the reporting kinds", "the run-start report names which kinds are unmetered"). No test in §10 exercises any of it: test 10 covers placeholders, test 11 covers a single runner's spend_key, test 44 covers the claude template's --agent. There is no test that a per-kind map routes `audit-role` to a different cmd, that `default` catches the unlisted kinds, that a map without `default` or a runner object without `cmd` exits 2, or that a mixed metered/unmetered map reports partial totals as partial.
suggestion: Add to §10.2: (a) a per-kind map routes each named kind to its own cmd and every unnamed kind to `default`, asserted from the seam's recorded invocations; (b) a map missing `default` and a runner object missing `cmd` each exit 2 before any child is spawned; (c) an object carrying `cmd` is read as a runner and one without it as a per-kind map; (d) under a mixed map, `run_max_budget_usd` accrues only the metered kinds and the run-start report names the unmetered ones.

finding: The re-run/skip rule is specified for role units only, but a re-run record unit destroys the work of the kinds that depend on it. §3.3 makes `audit-fix`'s durable write "that row carries a disposition" inside `$TP_ROUND_DIR/merged.ndjson`, and `review-resolve`'s durable write "every finding in `$TP_ROUND_DIR/merged.ndjson` carries a disposition" — both are in-place mutations of the file the record unit produces. §4.1 and §3.1.1 only say `next_units` omits roles whose findings file already satisfies the predicate; nothing says a `review-record`/`audit-record` unit whose durable write already exists is omitted. After a driver death (or a `no-units`/cap stop) mid-fix, the next run's record unit re-merges `role-*.ndjson` and overwrites `merged.ndjson`, silently discarding every disposition already written — and §10 test 36 actively describes that re-merge path as the desired behaviour.
suggestion: State the idempotence rule for every kind, not just roles: either the oracle omits any unit whose §3.3 predicate already holds (making the delete-before-spawn rule role-specific but the skip rule universal), or record units must merge non-destructively (preserve existing dispositions for rows that survive the re-merge). Add a test alongside 36 that a round with disposed rows is not re-merged into an undisposed `merged.ndjson`.

finding: Round 12's new test 55 promotes §6.3's unchanged prose ("may write exactly one path — their own findings file at $TP_ROUND_DIR/role-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson, plus the escalation record") into an asserted acceptance, but a shipped agent definition under .claude-plugin/agents/ is static: its permission rules cannot interpolate TP_ROUND_DIR/TP_UNIT_ID, so the best it can express is a glob over the rounds tree (every role's file in every round), not "the role's own findings file" — and the escalation record is written by the tp escalate subprocess through Bash, a channel a Write/Edit path allowlist never governs. As written, test 55 ("permit writing only ... and deny every other path") cannot be satisfied literally by the mechanism §6.3's own closing line names ("tool restrictions only"), while §6.2 states the only path-level enforcement the plugin ships is a four-pattern deny-list, not an allowlist.
suggestion: Restate test 55 against what a static definition can assert: the reviewer/auditor definitions allow the write tools only under the round-directory glob (e.g. Write/Edit on .tp/rounds/**) and deny every other write path, with the per-unit filename left to the prompt tp review/tp audit emits (§6.3); drop the escalation record from the write allowlist and note instead that it is written by tp escalate through the unit's Bash channel, which the allowlist does not gate.

finding: A unit's `id` is interpolated verbatim into filesystem paths — the log path `<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl` (§3.5) and the role findings file `role-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson` (§3.3, §6.2, §6.3) — but §3.1.1 defines ids that are not guaranteed path-safe: `audit-fix`'s id is `role:item_id` (a colon, and `item_id` is auditor-authored so it can carry `/`, spaces or a leading dot), and the `review-resolve`/`decompose` id is a spec base name. No sanitization, escaping or character restriction is stated, so no deterministic test can be written for an `audit-fix` unit's log path, and the Stop hook's path construction (§6.2) inherits the same ambiguity.
suggestion: Pin the rule in §3.1.1: either restrict ids to a stated character class, or state the exact transformation applied when an id becomes a path component (e.g. `:` and `/` replaced by `-`), and add a test that an `audit-fix` unit whose id contains `:` gets the documented log path.

finding: `TP_ROUND_DIR` is `.tp/rounds/<base>/<phase>-r$TP_ROUND`, and `TP_ROUND`/`TP_ROUND_DIR` are unset "when the oracle reports `round` null" (i.e. outside "a round-based phase", §4.1). Neither the set of `phase` tokens nor which of them are round-based is enumerated anywhere in the spec. Tests 37 (`TP_ROUND_DIR` "derived from phase and round", present "only in a round-based phase"), 46 and 36 therefore cannot be written to a fixed path: two engineers disagree on whether the implement and decompose phases are round-based and on the literal token (`review` vs `review-loop`).
suggestion: Enumerate the `phase` values `tp resume` reports and mark which are round-based (so `TP_ROUND` is non-null exactly there), and make test 37 assert one literal `TP_ROUND_DIR` value, e.g. `.tp/rounds/0.35.0/review-r3`.

finding: `seq` is load-bearing for two file paths — the log path `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl` (§3.5) and the escalation record `$TP_RUN_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-escalation.json` (§5.2) — but its form is never pinned: whether it starts at 0 or 1, whether it is zero-padded, and whether it is per-run monotonic across concurrent siblings in spawn order or assignment order. The run-state skeleton's `"seq": 0` is a JSON zero value, not a stated starting point. Tests 17 ("a retried unit gets a fresh log path"), 22 ("two concurrent siblings each write their own") and 37 (documented environment variables "in their documented forms") cannot assert a concrete filename; two engineers write `0-implement-x.jsonl` and `1-implement-x.jsonl`.
suggestion: State in §3.1.1 that `seq` is a decimal integer starting at 1, incremented per spawned attempt in spawn order and not zero-padded (or whatever the intended form is), and extend test 37 to assert `TP_UNIT_SEQ` for the first and second attempts of a run.

finding: §3.1.1 covers what a crashed `implement` unit leaves behind across runs ("leaves its task `wip`; the next run's `implement` unit resumes that same task") but not what a *retried* attempt inherits inside one run. A first attempt that edited files, failed the gate, and exited non-zero leaves a dirty working tree and possibly a partial commit; the second attempt starts a fresh process against that tree. Nothing says whether the driver cleans, whether the retry brief mentions the residue, or that the retry is expected to reconcile it. Test 17 covers only the fresh log path and the role-findings deletion, which is the analogous cleanup for role units — implying, but never stating, that `implement` has none.
suggestion: Add one sentence to §3.1.1: the driver never touches the working tree between attempts; a retried `implement` attempt inherits whatever the previous attempt left, and `last_failure` (§4.2) is the channel that tells it so. If instead a reset is intended, name the command and the safety condition.

finding: §3.1.1 introduces a fifth run-produced path under `.tp/` — the run lock at `.tp/locks/run-<base>.lock` — but the git-ignore surface enumerated for this release covers only four: test 15 (§10.2) lists `.tp/run-<base>.json`, `.tp/runs/`, `.tp/rounds/` and `.tp/last_failure-<base>.json`, and §10.7 states the `.tp/.gitignore` fixture 'gains four entries'. An unattended run therefore leaves a lock file showing in `git status` for the whole run, in exactly the phase where `implement` units are staging and committing — every such unit spends a round-trip deciding what the stray path is, and a sloppy `git add` sweeps it into a task-closing commit.
suggestion: Add `.tp/locks/` to the ignored set in test 15 and change §10.7 to five entries — or, if the shipped `.tp/.gitignore` already covers the lock directory, say so explicitly in §3.1.1 so the count in §10.7 is not read as the complete list.

finding: §3.1.1 introduces a new runtime artifact path, `.tp/locks/run-<base>.lock`, but it is absent from the git-ignore set the spec enumerates: test 15 names exactly `.tp/run-<base>.json`, `.tp/runs/`, `.tp/rounds/` and `.tp/last_failure-<base>.json`, and §10.7 pins that count at "four entries". Every other per-run artifact this version adds is declared git-ignored; the lock directory — which is created on every `tp run` and is machine-local by definition — would land in the working tree and be committed.
suggestion: Add `.tp/locks/` to the shipped `.tp/.gitignore`, update test 15 to five paths and §10.7 to "five entries", or state explicitly why the lock path is exempt.

finding: §3.2.2 says the driver "reads one number from the final line of that unit's log" using the declared `spend_key`, and covers only the case of a runner declaring no key (`spend: null`, `cap-budget` inert). It gives no behaviour for a runner that declares a key whose final log line is absent, is not JSON, lacks the key, or holds a non-numeric value — is that `spend: null`, a warning, or a failed attempt? Nor is the "dot path" grammar defined (nested objects only, or array indices too). Both decisions change whether `cap-budget` can ever trip, so an implementer cannot leave them to taste.
suggestion: Add: a declared `spend_key` that cannot be resolved from the final line records `spend_usd: null` for that unit, is reported once per run on stderr, and never fails the attempt; `spend_key` is a dot-separated path over JSON object keys only.

finding: Two durable-write predicates are satisfiable without the unit doing anything, and the spec does not say whether that counts as success. `review-resolve`'s is "Every finding in `$TP_ROUND_DIR/merged.ndjson` carries a disposition" — vacuously true when merged.ndjson holds zero findings, and undefined when the file is absent (contrast `review-record`, which explicitly requires existence). `decompose`'s is "The task file holds at least one task" — already true on any retry, or whenever the cycle re-decomposes a file that already holds tasks, so a decompose unit that imported nothing passes. §3.3's own claim that a predicate is "decidable by reading one file" holds, but test 18 only asserts decidability-without-a-baseline, never that the predicate separates a completed unit from a no-op.
suggestion: State in §3.3 whether an absent `merged.ndjson` fails or passes `review-resolve`, and give `decompose` a predicate a no-op cannot satisfy (e.g. the task file's task count is non-zero *and* the file's `imported_at`/mtime is newer than the round directory, or the oracle no longer reports a decompose unit). Add a test that a decompose unit which imports nothing over a non-empty task file is a failed attempt.

finding: §3.3 pins the `audit-fix` command surface in detail — `tp audit --resolve <results.ndjson> <idx> <fixed|wontfix|duplicate> "<evidence>"`, plus `--resolve-all` and `--force`, and a selector that is "a 0-based index or a `role:item_id` key" — but no test asserts any of it. Test 53's "dispose audit rows on the same terms as their review counterparts" delegates the whole contract to another command's behaviour, and neither selector form, the three disposition values, nor `--force` appears in an assertion. A rejected disposition value or a `role:item_id` selector that resolves to the wrong row would pass §10 as written.
suggestion: Add a §10.5 or §10.2 test that `tp audit --resolve` accepts each of the three dispositions, resolves the same row through both selector forms (index 0 and its `role:item_id`), rejects an out-of-range index and an unknown key as usage errors, and that `--resolve-all` disposes every row.

finding: "A unit is attempted `1 + run_max_unit_retries` times" fixes the count but not the schedule or the bookkeeping. Unspecified: (a) whether a failed attempt is re-spawned immediately, inside the same iteration (relevant when its concurrent siblings are still in flight), or is picked up by the next oracle poll; (b) where the attempt counter lives, given §3.1 forbids holding work in memory that could be re-derived and §3.5 forbids reading the run state back, so a driver that dies mid-unit has no disk record of attempts spent; (c) whether the attempt count is per `(kind, id)` for the whole run or per iteration.
suggestion: State that attempts are counted in the driver's memory per `(kind, id)` for the life of one run, that a retry is spawned within the same iteration after the failed attempt's siblings are joined (or explicitly on the next iteration), and that a new `tp run` starts the count fresh — the same restart rule §3.5 already gives the cap totals.

finding: `cap-units` is defined as "Spawned children reached `run_max_units`", but the overshoot paragraph grants a one-iteration overshoot only to wall-clock and budget: "a run can overshoot its wall-clock and budget caps by at most one iteration". For an iteration of 5 concurrent role units with 3 units of headroom left, the spec does not say whether the driver spawns all 5 (overshooting the unit cap) or spawns 3 and stops (leaving a half-collected round directory). The two choices differ observably in `totals.units` and in what the next run's oracle returns, and test 33 (all three counters agree) passes under either.
suggestion: Say in §3.4 whether the unit cap is checked per iteration like the others — recommended, since truncating a concurrent role set mid-round produces a partially collected round — and if so add it to the overshoot sentence; otherwise state that an iteration is never partially spawned and the cap is checked before the iteration.

finding: §3.4 says "Caps are evaluated between iterations only. Children already spawned run to completion, so a run can overshoot its wall-clock and budget caps by at most one iteration" — but `run_max_units` is overshootable on exactly the same terms and is not named. One iteration spawns a whole role fan-out (bounded only by the number of active roles for the phase, §3.3), so a run sitting one unit under `run_max_units` can spawn five more before the next cap check. The `cap-units` row ("Spawned children reached `run_max_units`") reads as a hard bound while the mechanism gives a soft one, and no test asserts either reading.
suggestion: Either extend the overshoot sentence to name `run_max_units` alongside wall-clock and budget, or state that the driver truncates a concurrent fan-out to the remaining unit allowance. Pin whichever it is in §10.1 test 3.

finding: The log path is `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl`, and §3.1.1 defines an `audit-fix` unit's id as the finding's `role:item_id`, with `review-resolve`/`decompose` ids being a spec base name. Those ids are agent- and corpus-authored strings that can contain `:`, `/`, spaces or `§`, so the derivation from id to filename is not total: a `/` in an `item_id` silently writes into a subdirectory that does not exist, and the child receives a `{log_path}` it cannot open. No sanitization or escaping rule is given, and `TP_UNIT_ID` is simultaneously used unescaped in `role-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson`.
suggestion: State the transform once: log filenames use the id with every character outside `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` replaced by `-` (the raw id stays in `TP_UNIT_ID` and in the run state row), and note that role ids are already constrained by the corpus so `role-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson` needs no transform.

finding: The run-state row rule is "Both writes are atomic (temp + rename), because concurrent siblings write rows in the same iteration." Temp+rename gives atomicity of a single replacement, not mutual exclusion: two sibling role units that each read `.tp/run-<base>.json`, append/update their own row and rename will silently lose whichever row landed first. Built exactly as written, a 5-role iteration can end with fewer than 5 rows and a wrong `totals.units`, and no test in §10.2 (12) would catch it because it only asserts one row's lifecycle.
suggestion: State the serialization explicitly: all run-state writes go through a single in-process mutex (or a single writer goroutine owning the file), with temp+rename only for crash-atomicity. Add a test asserting that N concurrent role units in one iteration produce N rows and a totals.units of N.

finding: §4.1 asserts "`next_units`, `round` and `phase` are the whole machine surface: the driver parses those three and nothing else", but two other sections require the driver to parse more. §3.2.2 has it read a spend key from the runner's log (acknowledged as an exception to Non-Goal 6, but not to this sentence), and §3.5 requires `tp run --status` to carry `spec_coverage_clean_rounds`, `role_streaks` and `divergence` "verbatim from `tp audit --status`" — a second tp command whose JSON the driver must invoke and parse, and the mechanism on which §1's central promise to the operator rests. The absolute claim in §4.1 and the requirement in §3.5 cannot both be literally true.
suggestion: Scope §4.1's sentence to the oracle ("of `tp resume --json`, the driver parses those three and nothing else") and state in §3.5 where the divergence signals come from — whether `tp run --status` shells out to `tp audit --status` or `tp resume --json` carries them through.

finding: `notify_cmd` is given a resolution rule with no writer. §7 says it "is per-operator rather than per-project and is read from `.tp/local.json` only", while `.tp/local.json` is otherwise the file tp itself manages (the `active` pointer and CLI-flag defaults) — no command in this spec, and none named from the existing surface, writes a `notify_cmd` into it. §5.1 compounds this by fencing the field ("under the variable a unit cannot set them at all, at any layer") and §10.5 test 40 asserts it "cannot be set at any layer", which presupposes a supported set path that exists when unattended mode is off.
suggestion: Name the supported write path — e.g. `tp config --set-local notify_cmd=…`, or an explicit "operators hand-edit `.tp/local.json`" — and make test 16's "`notify_cmd` is read from `.tp/local.json` only" exercise that path so the fence in test 40 has something to fence.

finding: §8a.5 justifies the arity change with "Every command's `Args` validator exits 2, matching §9's definition of a usage error". §9 is Non-Goals and contains no definition of a usage error — the exit-code semantics this argument rests on are in §3.4 ("2 on a usage error before the loop starts"). The load-bearing citation for a change that moves every existing arity test from exit 1 to exit 2 (§10.7) points at the wrong section.
suggestion: Repoint the reference to §3.4, or to whichever document actually defines the 0/1/2/3/4 table if the intent is to cite tp's existing exit-code contract rather than this spec.

finding: Test 53 is not a deterministic assertion and half of it is already test 18. "dispose audit rows on the same terms as their review counterparts" names no observable — an engineer must go read `tp review --resolve`'s tests to know what to assert, and "same terms" silently covers dispositions, selectors, `--force`, locking and output shape. Its second clause, "an `audit-fix` unit that disposes its row without a code change succeeds", restates test 18's "an `audit-fix` that closes its finding without a code change passes" verbatim in substance.
suggestion: Replace test 53 with the concrete assertions it stands for (dispositions accepted, both selector forms, `--resolve-all`, `--force`) and drop the duplicated no-code-change clause, leaving it in test 18 only.

finding: Step 4 reads "units marked concurrent together, every other kind alone", which reads as a per-unit marking carried in the driver's input, while §4.1 states the opposite — "Concurrency is not repeated per entry — it is fixed per kind by §3.3's table" — and test 38 pins `next_units` entries to exactly `{kind, id, brief_command}`. An engineer testing step 4 literally asserts a concurrency marker on the entry; an engineer testing §4.1 asserts its absence. The two tests contradict.
suggestion: Reword step 4 to "units whose kind §3.3 marks concurrent together, every other kind alone", so the marking is unambiguously a property of the kind and not of the `next_units` entry.

finding: §3.1 step 4 reads "Spawn a runner process per unit — units marked concurrent together, every other kind alone", which implies a per-entry concurrency marking on `next_units`. §4.1 explicitly denies one: "Concurrency is not repeated per entry — it is fixed per kind by §3.3's table", and §10.5 test 38 pins `next_units` entries to `{kind, id, brief_command}` with no concurrency field. The loop's own step description describes a payload shape the oracle contract forbids.
suggestion: Reword step 4 as "units whose kind §3.3 marks concurrent together, every other kind alone" so the marking is unambiguously a property of the kind, not of the entry.

finding: Of the eight variables §3.1.1 puts in every child's environment, `TP_RUN_ID` is the only one with no named consumer anywhere in the spec and it is literally `basename($TP_RUN_DIR)` — §3.1.1 defines `TP_RUN_DIR` as the absolute path of `.tp/runs/$TP_RUN_ID`. Every other variable is spent: `TP_UNIT_SEQ` names the escalation record (§5.2), `TP_UNIT_KIND`/`TP_UNIT_ID`/`TP_ROUND_DIR` are what the Stop hook and the role findings path are built from (§6.2, §6.3), `TP_FILE` is the resolved target. The one place `TP_RUN_ID` is read is `notify_cmd`'s environment (§5.2), which the driver sets separately and which is not a child unit. It is not free: it is a documented contract term that test 37 pins ('`TP_RUN_ID` a ULID'), so it costs a documented form and an assertion for a value no unit is described as using.
suggestion: Either name the child-side consumer that needs the id rather than the directory, or drop `TP_RUN_ID` from the child environment (keeping it for `notify_cmd`) and remove its clause from test 37 — a unit that wants the run id derives it from `TP_RUN_DIR`.

finding: §3.1.1 introduces a new on-disk path, `.tp/locks/run-<base>.lock`, held for the whole run. Test 15 enumerates the git-ignored set as `.tp/run-<base>.json`, `.tp/runs/`, `.tp/rounds/` and `.tp/last_failure-<base>.json`, and §10.7 confirms "The `.tp/.gitignore` fixture gains four entries" — so the lock directory is not covered. An unattended run therefore dirties the working tree with an untracked file for its whole duration, which is exactly the window in which `implement` units commit.
suggestion: Either add `.tp/locks/` as a fifth `.tp/.gitignore` entry (updating test 15 and §10.7's count), or state that the lock reuses an already-ignored location.

finding: Two sections combine into an unspecified path. §3.1.1 makes an `audit-fix` unit's id "the finding's `role:item_id`", and §3.5 builds each log path as `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl` — so a finding key becomes a filename component verbatim. Audit `item_id` values are role-authored strings (tp's own corpus produces things like section anchors), so they can carry `/`, `:` and whitespace, and the same id also expands into `{unit_id}` in a runner argv (§3.2). Nothing in the spec says whether the id is sanitized for the path, and §10.5 test 37's environment assertions do not reach it.
suggestion: State the sanitization rule once — e.g. the log path uses a slug of the id (non-`[A-Za-z0-9._-]` replaced), while `TP_UNIT_ID` and `{unit_id}` carry the raw id — and assert it for an `audit-fix` unit whose `item_id` contains a separator.

finding: `notify_cmd` is listed as a workflow field with a default and a range, but §7 then says it "is read from `.tp/local.json` only". The behaviour of the layers that are thereby dead is unspecified: does `tp set --workflow notify_cmd=…` (task override) or a `notify_cmd` in `.tp/config.json` fail as a usage error, or write a value that silently never resolves? `tp validate --project` and `tp config --extract` are said to cover the field "on the same terms as every existing workflow field", which for every other field means those layers are live. Test 16 asserts only that it is read from local.json.
suggestion: State the rule for the dead layers — recommended: `notify_cmd` in a task override or `.tp/config.json` is a validation error naming `.tp/local.json` — and extend test 16 to assert it, since a silently ignored notify command is undiagnosable in an unattended run.

finding: §7's Range column for `runner` reads "Built-in name or object", covering two of the three shapes §3.2 defines. The third — "a map from unit kind to either of those with a `default` key" — is the shape carrying the whole producer/judge separation argument, and it is also the shape with its own usage-error rule (a map missing `default`). A reader validating a config against §7's table alone has no reason to accept a per-kind map, and `tp validate --project` (§7) is specified to cover the new fields "on the same terms as every existing workflow field".
suggestion: Make the range "Built-in name, runner object, or per-kind map (§3.2)" so the validator's contract matches the three shapes §3.2 defines.
